I have read the relevant source material thoroughly. Here is a factual, chronological account.

## Source and what it actually describes

The reference is OpenAI's **GDPval** paper (arXiv 2510.04374v1), **Section 3.4 ("Increasing reasoning effort and scaffolding")** and **Appendix A.3 ("Additional Detail on Prompt-Tuning")**, with supporting context from **Section 3.3 ("Model strengths and weaknesses")**. Importantly, these sections do **not** narrate a single trajectory with one quoted task and a step-by-step tool log. They characterize a **population-level, recurring failure pattern** for the agent under analysis — GPT-5 at high reasoning effort, running in OpenAI's custom harness with web search and a code-interpreter container. I'll account for the facts as the source presents them.

## The task setup the agent operated in

- GDPval gives the model real-world, economically valuable occupational tasks. The agent is expected to produce **file deliverables** — the paper repeatedly names PDF, PPTX, DOCX, XLSX, MP4, and ZIP — inside its container, not merely text answers.
- Grading is by **blind pairwise human-expert comparison**: an expert sees the task prompt, reference files, and two unlabeled deliverables (one human-made, one model-made) and judges which is better.
- The agent under analysis ran with web search and a code-interpreter tool (the container where it builds and renders files).

## What the agent did, and where it went wrong (per Sections 3.3–3.4)

1. **It produced deliverables that contained obvious formatting defects.** Section 3.4 states plainly that "many of the observed GPT-5 failure modes were due to obvious formatting errors." Concretely:
   - **Black-square artifacts appeared in over half of the PDFs** GPT-5 generated.
   - **Egregious formatting errors affected 86% of generated PowerPoint (PPTX) files.**

2. **It submitted these deliverables without visually inspecting them.** A central observed behavior: before the remediation, agents used their **multimodal capabilities to inspect their own deliverables only 15% of the time.** In other words, the agent generated visual files (PDFs/slides) and shipped them without rendering and looking at them to catch the corruption.

3. **The feedback signal: experts preferred the human deliverable, and the loss was attributed to formatting.** Section 3.3 reports a clustering pipeline run over expert justifications. The result for this agent: **"GPT-5 high lost mainly from formatting errors and had the fewest instruction-following issues."** Unlike Gemini/Grok (which most often lost for failing to follow instructions, promising-but-not-delivering files, or wrong formats), and despite GPT-5 having relatively few accuracy/instruction errors, its deliverables were rejected primarily because they were visually broken.

## The remediation experiment documented in 3.4 / A.3

Having observed that the failures were "easy" formatting errors, the authors tested whether prompting and scaffolding could fix them:

- **The prompt (full text in Appendix A.3)** instructs the agent to: avoid the non-breaking hyphen U+2011 (use U+002D) and avoid emojis/nonstandard characters; make embedded graphics legible (≥ half page width); **always build PDFs with LibreOffice** (installing it if absent); use cross-platform fonts (Noto Sans/Serif) or embed fonts; keep deliverable text concise (≤ 4 sentences) and put deliverables in container files; and extract frames from videos to check for corruption.
- It mandates a **5-step pre-submission check**: (1) convert every visual deliverable to per-page/per-slide PNGs via LibreOffice; (2) **display** the PNGs and look for cut-off, overlapping, distorted, blank, or low-contrast content; (3) run programmatic checks for blank/overflowing/overlapping content and page limits; (4) match the deliverable against the prompt's stated requirements; (5) confirm exactly the right, non-corrupted files are being submitted — looping back if anything fails. Finally it appends a self-reported `CONFIDENCE[XX]`.
- **Scaffolding changes:** enabling GET requests in the container, and best-of-N sampling (**N = 4** submissions ranked by a GPT-5 judge).

## Outcome

- The intervention **fully eliminated the black-square artifacts** (previously in > half of PDFs).
- It **reduced egregious PowerPoint formatting errors from 86% to 64%.**
- Agent use of multimodal self-inspection **rose from 15% to 97%.**
- Human-preference win rate **improved by ~5 percentage points** (Figure 9(b)). Separately, higher reasoning effort (low→medium→high) also improved performance.
- Even after remediation, roughly **64% of PPTX files still had egregious formatting errors**, and GPT-5 continued to lose the majority of blind comparisons to human deliverables — the gains were real but partial.

A note on scope: because Sections 3.4 and A.3 report aggregate rates and a remediation experiment rather than one annotated run, the "task, tool calls, feedback" here are described at the level of the agent's typical behavior across GDPval tasks (generate a file deliverable in the container → submit without rendering it → expert prefers the human version, with the loss clustered as a formatting error), not a single quoted trajectory.

- [GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks (arXiv 2510.04374v1)](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.04374v1)
